newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan to sign EU accord at Malta conference.
newsitem.headline: Jordan to sign EU accord at Malta conference.

text.p: Jordan is expected to initial an association accord with the EU on the sidelines of the European-Mediterranean conference in Malta, paving the way for a reciprocal free trade zone by year 2010, officials said on Tuesday.

Jordanian officials said the accord will be initialed during the two-day conference which starts on Tuesday to discuss advancing the 27-member EU-Mediterranean partnership created in Barcelona in 1995.
Amman-based EU officials said the accord's signing follows the resolution of a host of disputes, including intellectual property rights and political matters.
It ends five tough rounds of talks since Jordan first opened discussions with Brussels in summer 1995.
The agreement, to be implemented on January 1 1999, will help speed up negotiations for a pact with the World Trade Organisation (WTO) by year-end.
Jordan receives over 30 percent of its imports from European Union countries. It hopes an association accord will boost capital inflows and direct investment into its aid-dependant economy.

Officials said they expect in return that the EU will keep its pledge of extra financial aid to ease the social impact on a majority of low income Jordanians of a difficult transitional period of accelerated free market reforms.
Under the accord Jordan agreed to four lists of goods which if supplied by EU countries will have import duties either totally eliminated or abolished over a period of from two to eight years.
A list of 492 industrial goods will have import duties lifted immediately the accord comes into effect.

A smaller non-exempt "negative" list includes cigarettes, alcholic beverages, small cars, used clothes, furniture and carpets. Officials say they secured this concession for both revenue purposes and to ensure protection for local industry.

The two sides finally reached a compromise over one of the thorniest issues surfacing in recent rounds which relates to the status of third country nationals and movement of illegal workers, mainly Palestinians and Iraqis, in Europe.

A declaration annexed to the accord will commit Jordan to adhering to international human rights conventions, replacing an earlier European insistence that Jordan takes responsiblity for any people entering the EU illegally from its territory.

A dispute over access of Jordanian tomato paste into the EU's farm market was also resolved by a concession which allows Jordan to raise its concentrate levels enabling it to add another 1,000 tonnes above a ceiling of 3,000 tonnes annually.

Jordan has pledged a phased liberalisation of government monopolies. While capital movement into Jordan will not be hampered, Amman was able to resist pressure for extra investment guarantees for European firms, officials said.
